en.title: Rank, Row Reduced Form and the Complete Solution of Ax = b
en.summary: This topic connects matrix transformations with linear systems by using Gauss-Jordan elimination to find the Reduced Row Echelon Form (RREF). Mastering this allows you to determine the rank, identify free variables, and write the complete solution as the sum of a particular solution and the null space.

sections.heading: Understanding RREF and Rank
sections.body: Think of row operations as rearranging equations without changing the underlying truth of the system. The **Reduced Row Echelon Form (RREF)** is the cleanest possible version of a matrix where every leading entry (pivot) is $1$, it is the only non-zero entry in its column, and all zero rows are pushed to the bottom. The **Rank** of a matrix, denoted as $\text{rank}(A)$, is simply the number of non-zero rows in its RREF, which equals the number of pivot columns. In semester exams, finding the rank is your first step to check if a system is consistent before even attempting to solve it.

sections.heading: The Step-by-Step Gauss-Jordan Algorithm
sections.body: To convert an augmented matrix $[A \mid b]$ to RREF and solve $Ax = b$, follow this strict algorithm: - Step 1: Write the augmented matrix $[A \mid b]$. - Step 2: Scan from left to right to find the first non-zero column. Swap rows if necessary to bring a non-zero entry to the top of this column (the pivot position). - Step 3: Use elementary row operations to create zeros below this pivot. - Step 4: Repeat for the next rows, moving diagonally down and right. - Step 5: Once you reach Row Echelon Form, work upwards to create zeros *above* each pivot and scale pivots to $1$, yielding the RREF.

sections.heading: Constructing the Complete Solution
sections.body: Once the system is in RREF, identify your pivot variables (columns with pivots) and free variables (columns without pivots). If the system is consistent (no row of the form $[0 \ 0 \ ... \ 0 \mid c]$ where $c \neq 0$), the **complete solution** is expressed as $x = x_p + x_n$. Here, $x_p$ is the particular solution obtained by setting all free variables to $0$, and $x_n$ is the null space solution obtained by turning off the right-hand side ($b = 0$) and assigning free parameters like $c_1, c_2$ to the free variables. This approach guarantees you capture every single solution to an underdetermined system.

key_terms.meaning: A matrix form with leading ones, zeros above and below pivots, and zero rows at the bottom.
The count of non-zero rows in the RREF or the number of pivot columns.
A variable corresponding to a column containing a leading one in the RREF.
A variable without a pivot column, which can take any real parameter value.
A specific solution vector $x_p$ found by setting all free variables to zero.
The homogeneous solution $x_n$ representing the kernel of the matrix.

example.title: Solving a 2x3 System
example.body: Consider the system $Ax = b$ where $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 & 3 \\ \end{bmatrix}$ and $b = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ \end{bmatrix}$. Step 1: Write augmented matrix $[A \mid b]$ as $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 & \mid & 1 \\ 2 & 4 & 3 & \mid & 3 \\ \end{bmatrix}$. Step 2: Apply $R_2 \leftarrow R_2 - 2R_1$ to get $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 & \mid & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & \mid & 1 \\ \end{bmatrix}$. Step 3: Apply $R_1 \leftarrow R_1 - R_2$ to clear above the pivot in column 3, yielding $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 & \mid & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & \mid & 1 \\ \end{bmatrix}$. Step 4: Identify pivots in columns $1$ and $3$. Variable $x_2$ is free. Step 5: For particular solution $x_p$, set $x_2 = 0$, giving $x_1 = 0$ and $x_3 = 1$, so $x_p = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ \end{bmatrix}$. Step 6: For null space, set $x_1 + 2x_2 = 0$ and $x_3 = 0$. Let $x_2 = c$, giving $x_n = c \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ \end{bmatrix}$. Complete solution is $x = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ \end{bmatrix} + c \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ \end{bmatrix}$.

exam_tips: Always check consistency using the augmented matrix rank ($r(A) = r(A \mid b)$) before writing down parametric solutions.
Clearly label which variables are pivot variables and which are free variables to secure full steps marks.
Do not stop at Row Echelon Form (REF) unless explicitly asked; RREF is required for reading off the complete solution directly.
Verify your particular solution by substituting it back into the original matrix equation $Ax_p = b$.
mistakes: Forgetting to perform row operations on the augmented column $b$ alongside matrix $A$.
Stopping elimination early when the matrix is only in upper triangular form instead of fully reduced RREF.
Writing the homogeneous solution without the arbitrary scalar constants like $c_1$ or $c_2$.
Swapping columns without keeping track of variable reordering.

en.title: Linear Independence, Basis and Dimension
en.summary: This topic forms the core of linear algebra, connecting matrix rank to vector space properties. Mastery of this is essential for solving homogeneous systems and scoring high in both semester exams and GATE.

sections.heading: Concept of Linear Independence
sections.body: A set of vectors $\{v_1, v_2, \dots, v_k\}$ in a vector space $V$ is linearly independent if the vector equation $c_1 v_1 + c_2 v_2 + \dots + c_k v_k = 0$ has only the trivial solution $c_1 = c_2 = \dots = c_k = 0$. If there exists a non-trivial solution where at least one $c_i \neq 0$, the vectors are linearly dependent. Analogy: Think of independent vectors as distinct directions on a map (like North and East). If a third vector points North-East, it lies in the plane of North and East, making it redundant or linearly dependent. In matrix terms, form a matrix $A$ with these vectors as columns and compute its rank. If $\text{rank}(A) = k$, the vectors are independent.

sections.heading: Basis of a Vector Space
sections.body: A set of vectors $B = \{v_1, v_2, \dots, v_n\}$ is called a basis for a vector space $V$ if two conditions are met: first, the vectors must be linearly independent, and second, they must span $V$. Spanning means that every vector in $V$ can be written as a linear combination of the basis vectors. In exam problems, to prove a set forms a basis for $\mathbb{R}^n$, place the vectors as columns of an $n \times n$ matrix and show that its determinant is non-zero, or equivalently, that its reduced row echelon form (RREF) is the identity matrix $I_n$.

sections.heading: Dimension and the Row/Column Spaces
sections.body: The dimension of a vector space $V$ is the number of vectors in any basis for $V$. For $\mathbb{R}^n$, the standard basis has $n$ vectors, so its dimension is $n$. According to Gilbert Strang, the fundamental theorem of linear algebra states that the dimension of the column space equals the dimension of the row space, known as the rank of the matrix. For an $m \times n$ matrix $A$, $\text{rank}(A) + \text{nullity}(A) = n$, where nullity is the dimension of the null space. When finding a basis for the column space of $A$, always select the pivot columns from the original matrix $A$, not from its row-reduced form.

key_terms.meaning: A set of vectors where no vector can be written as a linear combination of the others.
The solution where all coefficients in a linear combination equal zero.
The set of all possible linear combinations of a given set of vectors.
A linearly independent spanning set of a vector space.
The exact count of vectors present in any basis of the vector space.
The dimension of the null space of a matrix, representing the number of free variables.

example.title: Determining Basis and Dimension of a Vector Set
example.body: Consider three vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$: $v_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$, $v_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}$, and $v_3 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 2 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}$. Step 1: Form the matrix $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$ using these vectors as columns. Step 2: Perform row operations to find the rank. Subtract $2R_1$ from $R_2$ and $R_1$ from $R_3$, yielding $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & -2 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$. Step 3: Subtract $R_2$ from $R_3$ to get $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$. Step 4: Count the pivots. There are 2 pivot columns (column 1 and column 2). Therefore, the rank is 2. Step 5: Conclude that the dimension of the subspace spanned by these vectors is 2, and a basis is given by the original pivot columns $\{v_1, v_2\}$.

exam_tips: - Always use the original matrix columns when stating the basis for a column space, never the columns of the RREF matrix.
- To check if $n$ vectors form a basis for $\mathbb{R}^n$, compute the determinant; if $\det(A) \neq 0$, they form a basis.
- Remember the Rank-Nullity Theorem ($\text{rank} + \text{nullity} = n$) as it frequently appears in 5-mark and 10-mark questions.
- Write down the definition of linear independence clearly before setting up the augmented matrix.
mistakes: - Selecting basis vectors from the reduced row echelon form (RREF) instead of the original matrix.
- Confusing dimension with the number of vectors in a linearly dependent set.
- Forgetting to check if the matrix is square before calculating the determinant.
en.diagram: A 3D coordinate system showing two non-collinear vectors defining a plane (basis of dimension 2) and a third vector lying within that same plane.

en.title: The Four Fundamental Subspaces and Invertible Matrices
en.summary: Every $m \times n$ matrix gives birth to four fundamental subspaces: the column space, row space, null space, and left null space. Mastering their bases and dimensions is vital for solving linear systems and scoring high in university exams and GATE.

sections.heading: The Anatomy of Four Subspaces
sections.body: Think of a matrix $A$ of size $m \times n$ as a linear transformation from $\mathbb{R}^n$ to $\mathbb{R}^m$. The four fundamental subspaces are tied to this mapping. The **row space** $C(A^T)$ lives in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and is spanned by the rows of $A$. Its dimension is the rank $r$. The **null space** $N(A)$ also lives in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and consists of all solutions to $Ax = 0$; its dimension is $n - r$. On the output side, the **column space** $C(A)$ lives in $\mathbb{R}^m$ with dimension $r$, while the **left null space** $N(A^T)$ lives in $\mathbb{R}^m$ satisfying $A^Ty = 0$ with dimension $m - r$. Gilbert Strang emphasizes that these spaces are orthogonal complements in their respective domains.

sections.heading: Algorithm to Find Row Space and Left Null Space
sections.body: To find the row space and left null space, perform Gaussian elimination to reduce $A$ to its Row Canonical Form or Reduced Row Echelon Form (RREF), denoted as $R$. **Step 1:** Write down the augmented matrix $[A \mid I]$ where $I$ is the $m \times m$ identity matrix. **Step 2:** Apply elementary row operations until $A$ becomes $R$. The resulting matrix has the form $[R \mid E]$, where $E A = R$. **Step 3:** The non-zero rows of $R$ form a basis for the **row space** $C(A^T)$. **Step 4:** The rows of $E$ corresponding to the zero rows of $R$ form a basis for the **left null space** $N(A^T)$, because if row $i$ of $R$ is all zeros, the corresponding row $y^T$ of $E$ satisfies $y^T A = 0$.

sections.heading: Invertible Matrices and the Big Picture
sections.body: An $n \times n$ square matrix $A$ is **invertible** if and only if it has full rank $r = n$. In this special case, the four subspaces collapse to trivial or full dimensions. The row space and column space are the entire space $\mathbb{R}^n$. The null space and left null space contain only the zero vector: $N(A) = \{0\}$ and $N(A^T) = \{0\}$. For an invertible matrix, the determinant is non-zero, $\det(A) \neq 0$, and the inverse $A^{-1}$ exists such that $A A^{-1} = I$. Examiners love testing this equivalence: full rank means invertible means independent columns means zero null space.

key_terms.meaning: Subspace spanned by the rows of a matrix, denoted $C(A^T)$.
Null space of $A^T$, satisfying $A^Ty = 0$, denoted $N(A^T)$.
The dimension of the row space or column space, denoted $r$.
Reduced Row Echelon Form used to systematically find bases.
A square matrix with full rank and a unique inverse.

example.title: Finding Row Space and Left Null Space for a 2x3 Matrix
example.body: Let $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 4 & 6 \end{bmatrix}$. We set up $[A \mid I_2] = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 4 & 6 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$. Subtract $2 \times$ row 1 from row 2. We get $R = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, where $E = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$. The **row space** is spanned by the non-zero row of $R$: $\left\{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \right\}$. The **left null space** is spanned by the row of $E$ where $R$ has a zero row, which is $\left\{ \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \right\}$. Notice that $m = 2, n = 3, r = 1$. Row space dimension is $1$, left null space dimension is $m - r = 2 - 1 = 1$.

exam_tips: Always state the dimensions of the subspaces using the rank-nullity theorem before writing the bases.
When finding the left null space using $[A \mid I]$, remember that the bottom rows of the transformed $I$ matrix correspond to the zero rows of RREF.
For GATE, memorize the equivalences: $A$ is invertible $\iff$ rank is $n$ $\iff$ $N(A) = \{0\}$.
mistakes: Using the columns of the original matrix $A$ instead of the RREF matrix when asked for a row space basis.
Confusing the left null space $N(A^T)$ with the standard null space $N(A)$.
Forgetting that left null space vectors are row vectors multiplying $A$ from the left ($y^T A = 0$).
en.diagram: A 2D schematic showing two orthogonal pairs of fundamental subspaces: row space orthogonal to null space in $\mathbb{R}^n$, and column space orthogonal to left null space in $\mathbb{R}^m$.

en.title: Orthogonal Vectors and Orthogonal Subspaces
en.summary: Vectors are orthogonal when their dot product is zero, extending the concept of perpendicularity to n-dimensional space. Orthogonal subspaces, such as the row space and nullspace of a matrix, are fundamental to solving inconsistent systems and form the core of Strang's Four Fundamental Subspaces.

sections.heading: The Core Idea: Orthogonal Vectors
sections.body: Think of the floor and a wall in your room: they meet at a right angle, completely independent of each other's directions. In linear algebra, two vectors $x$ and $y$ in $R^n$ are orthogonal if their inner product (dot product) is zero, written as $x^T y = 0$. This implies the Pythagorean theorem holds: $\|x + y\|^2 = \|x\|^2 + \|y\|^2$. Imagine a right-angled triangle where the legs are orthogonal vectors and the hypotenuse is their sum. In B.Tech semester exams, proving two vectors or eigenvectors are orthogonal is a standard 5-mark question, usually solved by simply taking their dot product and showing it evaluates to zero.

sections.heading: Orthogonal Subspaces and Fundamental Theorem
sections.body: We extend orthogonality from individual vectors to entire subspaces. Two subspaces $V$ and $W$ of $R^n$ are orthogonal if every vector $v$ in $V$ is orthogonal to every vector $w$ in $W$. The most crucial application in GATE and university exams is Gilbert Strang's Fundamental Subspace Theorem: The row space of a matrix $A$ (size $m \times n$) is orthogonal to its nullspace, and the column space is orthogonal to the left nullspace. Mathematically, $row(A) \perp null(A)$ in $R^n$. This means if $Ax = 0$, every row vector of $A$ has a zero dot product with the solution vector $x$.

sections.heading: Algorithm to Find Orthogonal Complements
sections.body: To find the orthogonal complement of a subspace spanned by given vectors, follow this step-by-step algorithm: First, form a matrix $A$ where the given basis vectors are its rows. Second, find the nullspace of $A$ by solving the homogeneous system $Ax = 0$ using Gauss-Jordan elimination. Third, write the general solution in parametric vector form. The vectors forming these parameters serve as the basis for the orthogonal complement subspace. Always verify your result by taking the dot product of your original basis vectors with the newly found complement basis vectors to ensure you get zero.

key_terms.meaning: Vectors whose dot product is zero, representing a 90-degree angle between them.
Subspaces where every vector in the first is perpendicular to every vector in the second.
The space of all vectors orthogonal to a given subspace, denoted as $V^\perp$.
The subspace spanned by the rows of a matrix, orthogonal to its nullspace.
The set of all solutions to the homogeneous equation $Ax = 0$.

example.title: Finding the Orthogonal Complement of a Subspace
example.body: Step 1: Let subspace $V$ be spanned by the row vector $v = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & -3 \end{bmatrix}$. We want to find its orthogonal complement in $R^3$. Step 2: Set up the matrix $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & -3 \end{bmatrix}$. We need to solve $Ax = 0$ to find the nullspace. Step 3: Write the equation $1x_1 + 2x_2 - 3x_3 = 0$. Step 4: Choose free variables for $x_2$ and $x_3$. Let $x_2 = s$ and $x_3 = t$. Then $x_1 = -2s + 3t$. Step 5: Express the solution vector $x = \begin{bmatrix} -2s + 3t \\ s \\ t \end{bmatrix} = s \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} + t \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$. Step 6: The basis for the orthogonal complement is \begin{Bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \end{Bmatrix}. Check: $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & -3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} = -2 + 2 + 0 = 0$ (verified).

exam_tips: Always state the dimension theorem explicitly: $dim(row(A)) + dim(null(A)) = n$ to secure full marks.
When asked for an orthogonal complement, remember it is equivalent to finding the nullspace of the matrix formed by the given basis vectors.
Cross-verify your final answer by taking the dot product between the original vectors and the derived orthogonal vectors; it must be zero.
mistakes: Confusing the orthogonal complement with a single random perpendicular vector instead of the entire subspace.
Forgetting to reduce the matrix to row echelon form before reading off the free variables for the nullspace.
Mixing up column space orthogonality with row space orthogonality.
en.diagram: A 3D Cartesian coordinate system showing a 2D plane (representing the row space) intersected perpendicularly by a 1D line passing through the origin (representing the nullspace).

en.title: Projections and Least Squares
en.summary: We study how to project vectors onto subspaces using projection matrices and how to solve overdetermined systems $Ax = b$ approximately using Least Squares. This is a vital topic for both semester exams and GATE, frequently appearing as numerical matrix calculations.

sections.heading: Analogy and Core Idea
sections.body: Imagine standing directly under a street light: your shadow on the ground is your orthogonal projection. In linear algebra, if a vector $b$ does not lie in the column space $C(A)$, we cannot solve $Ax = b$. The closest vector to $b$ that we *can* reach in $C(A)$ is its projection $p$. The error vector $e = b - p$ must be perpendicular (orthogonal) to the column space of $A$, leading directly to the normal equations.

sections.heading: The Projection Matrix
sections.body: To project any vector $b$ onto the column space of a matrix $A$, we use the projection matrix $P$. If $A$ has linearly independent columns, the projection matrix is given by $P = A(A^T A)^{-1} A^T$. - Notice that $P$ satisfies two key properties for exams: $P^2 = P$ (idempotent) and $P^T = P$ (symmetric). Multiplying any vector $b$ by $P$ yields the projected vector $p = Pb$.

sections.heading: Least Squares Algorithm
sections.body: When $Ax = b$ has no exact solution because $b$ is outside $C(A)$, we find the best approximate solution $\hat{x}$ by minimizing the squared error $\|Ax - b\|^2$. - Step 1: Write down the coefficient matrix $A$ and vector $b$. - Step 2: Compute $A^T A$ and $A^T b$. - Step 3: Set up the normal equations $A^T A \hat{x} = A^T b$. - Step 4: Solve this linear system for $\hat{x}$ using Gaussian elimination or inverse. The resulting $\hat{x}$ is the least squares solution.

key_terms.meaning: A square matrix $P$ that projects vectors onto a subspace, satisfying $P^2 = P$ and $P^T = P$.
The subspace of all vectors orthogonal to every vector in a given subspace.
The system $A^T A \hat{x} = A^T b$ used to find the least squares solution.
The minimum distance vector $e = b - A\hat{x}$ which is perpendicular to the column space.

example.title: Finding the Least Squares Line
example.body: Find the least squares solution $\hat{x} = \begin{bmatrix} C \\ D \end{bmatrix}$ for the data points $(0, 1), (1, 3), (2, 2)$. - Step 1: Set up $Ax = b$ where equations are $C + 0D = 1$, $C + D = 3$, $C + 2D = 2$. Thus $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$ and $b = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}$. - Step 2: Compute $A^T A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 3 \\ 3 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$ and $A^T b = \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix}$. - Step 3: Solve $\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 3 \\ 3 & 5 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} C \\ D \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix}$. - Step 4: Subtract row 1 from row 2 to get $2D = 1$, so $D = 0.5$. Substitute back: $3C + 3(0.5) = 6 \implies 3C = 4.5 \implies C = 1.5$. The best fit line is $y = 1.5 + 0.5t$.

exam_tips: Always verify your normal equations $A^T A \hat{x} = A^T b$ before solving to avoid silly arithmetic errors.
Remember that the error vector $e = b - A\hat{x}$ must satisfy $A^T e = 0$ (it is in the left nullspace).
In university exams, show all intermediate matrix multiplications clearly step by step to secure partial marking.
mistakes: Trying to compute $A^{-1}$ when $A$ is not a square matrix (use $A^T A$ instead).
Confusing the projection matrix $P = A(A^T A)^{-1} A^T$ with just $(A^T A)^{-1} A^T$.
Forgetting to check if columns of $A$ are linearly independent before inverting $A^T A$.
en.diagram: A 3D coordinate system showing a plane $C(A)$, a vector $b$ sticking out of the plane, its drop-down projection $p$ on the plane, and the orthogonal error vector $e = b - p$ forming a right angle with the plane.

en.title: Orthonormal Bases and Gram-Schmidt (A = QR)
en.summary: Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization transforms any linearly independent set of vectors into an orthonormal basis, directly enabling the $A = QR$ matrix factorization. This is a high-scoring numerical topic in semester exams and vital for least-squares problems in GATE.

sections.heading: Introduction to Orthonormal Sets
sections.body: Think of an orthonormal basis like a standard 3D Cartesian coordinate system ($i, j, k$): all vectors are mutually orthogonal (at 90 degrees) and have a unit length of 1. Mathematically, a set of vectors $\{q_1, q_2, \dots, q_n\}$ is orthonormal if $q_i^T q_j = 0$ for $i \neq j$ and $q_i^T q_i = 1$. Working with orthonormal matrices ($Q^T Q = I$) prevents round-off errors in computers and simplifies projections immensely. In exams, you must always check unit length before declaring a basis orthonormal.

sections.heading: The Gram-Schmidt Algorithm
sections.body:
Given a set of linearly independent vectors $\{x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n\}$, Gram-Schmidt constructs an orthogonal set $\{v_1, v_2, \dots, v_n\}$ and then normalizes them to get $\{q_1, q_2, \dots, q_n\}$. 
- Step 1: Set $v_1 = x_1$ and normalize $q_1 = v_1 / \|v_1\|$. 
- Step 2: For the next vector $x_2$, subtract its projection onto the previously computed $q_1$: $v_2 = x_2 - (x_2^T q_1)q_1$. Then normalize $q_2 = v_2 / \|v_2\|$. 
- General Step: $v_k = x_k - \sum_{j=1}^{k-1} (x_k^T q_j)q_j$, followed by $q_k = v_k / \|v_k\|$. Always carry fractions carefully to avoid messy square roots.

sections.heading: The A = QR Factorization
sections.body: Any real $m \times n$ matrix $A$ with linearly independent columns can be factored into $A = QR$. Here, $Q$ is an $m \times n$ matrix with orthonormal columns formed by the Gram-Schmidt process, and $R$ is an $n \times n$ upper triangular matrix. Because $Q^T Q = I$, you can easily find $R$ by multiplying both sides by $Q^T$, yielding $R = Q^T A$. This factorization is heavily tested in GATE because it simplifies solving least-squares equations $A^x = b$ into the easily solvable triangular system $R x = Q^T b$.

key_terms.meaning: A basis consisting of mutually orthogonal vectors, each having a magnitude of one.
An algorithm to convert a linearly independent set into an orthogonal or orthonormal set.
The shadow or component of one vector lying along the direction of another vector.
Decomposition of a matrix $A$ into an orthogonal matrix $Q$ and an upper triangular matrix $R$.
A square matrix where all entries below the main diagonal are zero.

example.title: Finding QR Factorization for a 3x2 Matrix
example.body:
Let $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$. Let $x_1$ be the first column and $x_2$ be the second column. 
Step 1: Orthogonalize $x_1$. 
$v_1 = x_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$. 
The norm $\|v_1\| = \sqrt{1^2 + 0^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{2}$. 
$q_1 = v_1 / \|v_1\| = \begin{bmatrix} 1/\sqrt{2} \\ 0 \\ 1/\sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix}$. 
Step 2: Orthogonalize $x_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$. 
Compute projection scalar: $x_2^T q_1 = (1)(1/\sqrt{2}) + (1)(0) + (0)(1/\sqrt{2}) = 1/\sqrt{2}$. 
$v_2 = x_2 - (x_2^T q_1)q_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} - (1/\sqrt{2})\begin{bmatrix} 1/\sqrt{2} \\ 0 \\ 1/\sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 1/2 \\ 0 \\ 1/2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1/2 \\ 1 \\ -1/2 \end{bmatrix}$. 
Step 3: Normalize $v_2$. 
$\|v_2\| = \sqrt{(1/2)^2 + 1^2 + (-1/2)^2} = \sqrt{1/4 + 1 + 1/4} = \sqrt{6/4} = \sqrt{6}/2$. 
$q_2 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}/2} \begin{bmatrix} 1/2 \\ 1 \\ -1/2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1/\sqrt{6} \\ 2/\sqrt{6} \\ -1/\sqrt{6} \end{bmatrix}$. 
Thus, $Q = \begin{bmatrix} 1/\sqrt{2} & 1/\sqrt{6} \\ 0 & 2/\sqrt{6} \\ 1/\sqrt{2} & -1/\sqrt{6} \end{bmatrix}$. 
Step 4: Compute $R = Q^T A$. 
$R = \begin{bmatrix} 1/\sqrt{2} & 0 & 1/\sqrt{2} \\ 1/\sqrt{6} & 2/\sqrt{6} & -1/\sqrt{6} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \sqrt{2} & 1/\sqrt{2} \\ 0 & \sqrt{6}/2 \end{bmatrix}$. 
Final check: $QR = A$ holds true.

exam_tips: Always normalize your vectors at each step if the question asks for an orthonormal basis, not just an orthogonal one.
Double-check your $R$ matrix using $R = Q^T A$ instead of calculating elements individually to save time and avoid arithmetic errors.
In GATE, remember that if $A$ is square, $Q$ is an orthogonal matrix where $Q^{-1} = Q^T$.
Neatly rationalize denominators where possible, but leaving $\sqrt{2}$ in intermediate steps is completely acceptable and safer.
mistakes: Forgetting to subtract projections from ALL preceding $q$ vectors when computing $v_k$ for $k > 2$.
Using the raw orthogonal vector $v_k$ instead of the normalized unit vector $q_k$ during the subtraction step.
Confusing the dimensions of $Q$ and $R$; $Q$ has the same dimensions as $A$ ($m \times n$), while $R$ is square ($n \times n$).

en.title: Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors
en.summary: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors represent the fundamental characteristic roots and invariant directions of a linear transformation, serving as the core mathematical machinery behind PageRank, PCA, and SVD. For B.Tech semester exams and GATE, this topic is a goldmine for predictable numerical questions involving characteristic equations and diagonalisation.

sections.heading: The Core Idea and Definition
sections.body: Imagine stretching a rubber sheet; most vectors get rotated and scaled, but a few special vectors only change in length, not direction. These are the eigenvectors, and their scaling factors are the eigenvalues. Mathematically, for a square matrix $A$, a non-zero vector $v$ and a scalar $\lambda$ satisfy the equation $Av = \lambda v$. This means multiplying the matrix $A$ by the vector $v$ has the exact same effect as simply scaling $v$ by the scalar $\lambda$. In linear algebra, this reduces complicated matrix powers $A^k$ to simple scalar powers $\lambda^k$, which is why it is heavily tested in engineering mathematics.

sections.heading: Step-by-Step Algorithm for Finding Eigenvalues
sections.body: To find the eigenvalues of an $n \times n$ matrix $A$, we start from the fundamental relation $Av = \lambda v$, which can be rewritten as $(A - \lambda I)v = 0$. For a non-trivial solution $v \neq 0$ to exist, the matrix $(A - \lambda I)$ must be singular, meaning its determinant must be zero. Thus, the characteristic equation is given by $\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$. Solving this polynomial equation of degree $n$ yields $n$ eigenvalues. Always check your work using two standard matrix properties: the sum of the eigenvalues equals the trace of $A$ (sum of main diagonal elements), and the product of the eigenvalues equals the determinant $\det(A)$.

sections.heading: Step-by-Step Algorithm for Finding Eigenvectors
sections.body: Once you obtain an eigenvalue $\lambda_i$, substitute it back into the homogeneous system $(A - \lambda_i I)v = 0$. Solve this system of linear equations using Gaussian elimination to find the null space. The non-zero free vectors form the basis for the eigenspace corresponding to $\lambda_i$. If an eigenvalue has an algebraic multiplicity greater than one, you must check if its geometric multiplicity (the dimension of the null space) matches. If it does not, the matrix is defective and cannot be diagonalised. For distinct eigenvalues, eigenvectors are guaranteed to be linearly independent.

key_terms.meaning: A scalar $\lambda$ satisfying $\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$.
A non-zero vector $v$ satisfying $Av = \lambda v$.
The polynomial equation $\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$ used to find eigenvalues.
The sum of main diagonal elements of a square matrix, equal to the sum of its eigenvalues.
The number of times an eigenvalue is repeated as a root of the characteristic polynomial.
The dimension of the eigenspace for a specific eigenvalue, representing the number of linearly independent eigenvectors.

example.title: Finding Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors of a 2x2 Matrix
example.body: Let $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$. Step 1: Form $A - \lambda I = \begin{bmatrix} 2 - \lambda & 1 \\ 1 & 2 - \lambda \end{bmatrix}$. Step 2: Compute the determinant $\det(A - \lambda I) = (2 - \lambda)^2 - (1)(1) = 0$. Expanding this gives $\lambda^2 - 4\lambda + 3 = 0$. Factoring yields $(\lambda - 1)(\lambda - 3) = 0$, so the eigenvalues are $\lambda_1 = 1$ and $\lambda_2 = 3$. Step 3: For $\lambda_1 = 1$, solve $(A - I)v = 0$, which gives $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$. This yields $x + y = 0$, so choosing $x = 1$ gives the eigenvector $v_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}$. Step 4: For $\lambda_2 = 3$, solve $(A - 3I)v = 0$, giving $\begin{bmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$. This yields $-x + y = 0$, so choosing $x = 1$ gives the eigenvector $v_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$.

exam_tips: Always verify your eigenvalues using Trace = Sum of roots and Determinant = Product of roots before finding eigenvectors.
For symmetric matrices ($A = A^T$), eigenvectors corresponding to distinct eigenvalues are always orthogonal; use this to cross-verify your answers in GATE.
When finding eigenvectors for repeated eigenvalues, carefully find the rank of $(A - \lambda I)$ to ensure correct geometric multiplicity.
mistakes: Subtracting $\lambda$ from off-diagonal elements instead of only the main diagonal elements when forming $A - \lambda I$.
Forgetting to normalise eigenvectors when required, or writing dependent vectors for a repeated eigenvalue.
Arithmetic sign errors while expanding the characteristic determinant, especially for $3 \times 3$ matrices.
en.diagram: A 2D coordinate plane showing a matrix transformation stretching the unit vector along a specific diagonal axis without changing its direction, labeled as the eigenvector with scaling factor $\lambda$.

en.title: Diagonalization ($A = S\Lambda S^{-1}$) and Powers of a Matrix
en.summary: Diagonalization breaks a complex matrix operation into independent scalar stretches along principal directions, making high powers like $A^{100}$ trivial to compute. It is heavily tested in university semester exams and GATE for its direct link to eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and system dynamics.

sections.heading: The Core Idea and Real-World Analogy
sections.body: Think of a square matrix $A$ as a complicated machine that distorts space. If you look at it from standard Cartesian coordinates, every vector changes both its length and direction in a messy way. **Diagonalization** means finding a special set of directions—the eigenvectors—where the matrix's action is purely stretching or shrinking without any rotation. **Analogy**: Imagine stretching a rubber sheet. If you pull along its natural grain (eigenvectors), points just move outward by a factor $\lambda$. Diagonalization is simply changing your viewpoint to align with this natural grain so that math becomes uncoupled and trivial.

sections.heading: Step-by-Step Algorithm for Diagonalization
sections.body: To diagonalize an $n \times n$ matrix $A$, follow these strict algorithmic steps. First, **compute the characteristic polynomial** by solving $\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$ to find the eigenvalues $\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \dots, \lambda_n$. Second, **find the eigenvectors** for each distinct eigenvalue by solving $(A - \lambda_i I)x = 0$ to get a basis for each eigenspace. Third, **construct the modal matrix $S$** by placing these eigenvectors as its columns in the exact same order as their corresponding eigenvalues appear in $\Lambda$. Fourth, **form the diagonal matrix $\Lambda$** with the eigenvalues on the main diagonal. Finally, **verify invertibility**: $A$ is diagonalizable if and only if $S$ has linearly independent columns (i.e., $\det(S) \neq 0$). If an eigenvalue of algebraic multiplicity $k$ does not yield $k$ linearly independent eigenvectors, the matrix is **defective** and cannot be diagonalized.

sections.heading: Computing Powers of a Matrix ($A^k$)
sections.body: Once a matrix is factored as $A = S\Lambda S^{-1}$, computing high powers like $A^k$ becomes computationally instantaneous. **The derivation** is straightforward: $A^2 = (S\Lambda S^{-1})(S\Lambda S^{-1}) = S\Lambda (S^{-1}S) \Lambda S^{-1} = S\Lambda^2 S^{-1}$. By induction, $A^k = S\Lambda^k S^{-1}$. **Why this matters**: Raising a diagonal matrix $\Lambda^k$ only requires raising each individual diagonal entry to the power $k$, completely avoiding expensive matrix-matrix multiplications. This technique is extensively used in solving linear recurrence relations, Fibonacci sequences, and discrete Markov chains in computer science.

key_terms.meaning: A scalar $\lambda$ satisfying $Ax = \lambda x$ for a non-zero vector $x$
A non-zero vector $x$ that only changes by a scalar factor under linear transformation $A$
The polynomial equation $\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$ used to find eigenvalues
A square matrix whose columns are the linearly independent eigenvectors of $A$
A diagonal matrix containing the eigenvalues of $A$ on its main diagonal
A square matrix that lacks a full set of linearly independent eigenvectors and cannot be diagonalized

example.title: Diagonalizing $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$ and finding $A^3$
example.body: Step 1: Find eigenvalues. Compute $\det(A - \lambda I) = \det \begin{bmatrix} 1-\lambda & 2 \\ 0 & 3-\lambda \end{bmatrix} = (1-\lambda)(3-\lambda) = 0$. The eigenvalues are $\lambda_1 = 1$ and $\lambda_2 = 3$. Step 2: Find eigenvectors. For $\lambda_1 = 1$, solve $(A - I)x = 0$, giving $\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$, which yields $x_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$. For $\lambda_2 = 3$, solve $(A - 3I)x = 0$, giving $\begin{bmatrix} -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$, which yields $x_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$. Step 3: Form $S$ and $\Lambda$. $S = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ and $\Lambda = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$. Step 4: Find $S^{-1}$. $S^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$. Step 5: Compute $A^3$. $A^3 = S\Lambda^3 S^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1^3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3^3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 27 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 26 \\ 0 & 27 \end{bmatrix}$.

exam_tips: Always write the matching order: if $\lambda_1$ is the first column of $S$, its eigenvalue must be the first element in $\Lambda$.
Check if $\det(S) \neq 0$ before concluding the matrix is diagonalizable to avoid losing marks on defective matrices.
When computing powers like $A^{10}$, never multiply $A$ ten times; always expand using $S\Lambda^{10}S^{-1}$.
mistakes: Swapping the order of eigenvalues in $\Lambda$ without reordering the eigenvectors in $S$.
Forgetting to invert matrix $S$ at the end of the $S\Lambda^kS^{-1}$ formula.
Assuming every square matrix is diagonalizable (forgetting to check geometric vs. algebraic multiplicity).

en.title: Symmetric Matrices and the Spectral Decomposition
en.summary: Symmetric matrices are fundamental in linear algebra because they guarantee real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors. The spectral decomposition allows us to express such a matrix as a linear combination of its projection matrices, which is heavily tested in university exams and GATE.

sections.heading: Core Idea and Real-World Analogy
sections.body: Think of a symmetric matrix $A = A^T$ like a set of pure, mutually perpendicular axes in space. Just as any 3D shape can be rotated to align with the standard Cartesian coordinate axes, a symmetric matrix can be rotated via its orthogonal eigenvectors so that it becomes completely diagonal. In the real world, this is like principal component analysis (PCA) in data science, where correlated variables are transformed into uncorrelated principal axes that capture maximum variance.

sections.heading: Properties of Symmetric Matrices
sections.body: For any real symmetric matrix $A$ of size $n \times n$, two major properties hold: first, all its eigenvalues are guaranteed to be real numbers. Second, eigenvectors corresponding to distinct eigenvalues are automatically orthogonal. If an eigenvalue has algebraic multiplicity greater than one, we use the Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization process to make the corresponding eigenvectors orthonormal. Thus, we can always find an orthogonal matrix $Q$ and a diagonal matrix $\Lambda$ such that $A = Q \Lambda Q^T$.

sections.heading: Step-by-Step Algorithm for Spectral Decomposition
sections.body:
- Step 1: Find the characteristic polynomial by solving $\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$ to get the eigenvalues $\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \dots, \lambda_n$.
- Step 2: For each eigenvalue $\lambda_i$, solve $(A - \lambda_i I)x = 0$ to find the corresponding eigenvectors.
- Step 3: If eigenvalues repeat, use Gram-Schmidt on the basis of the eigenspace to ensure the eigenvectors are mutually orthogonal.
- Step 4: Normalize every eigenvector to unit length so that $\|x_i\| = 1$.
- Step 5: Form the orthogonal matrix $Q = \begin{bmatrix} x_1 & x_2 & \dots & x_n \end{bmatrix}$ and diagonal matrix $\Lambda = \text{diag}(\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \dots, \lambda_n)$. The spectral decomposition is $A = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lambda_i x_i x_i^T$.

key_terms.meaning: A square matrix $A$ that is equal to its transpose, $A = A^T$.
The theorem stating that every real symmetric matrix can be diagonalized by an orthogonal matrix of its eigenvectors.
A square matrix $Q$ whose columns and rows are orthonormal vectors, satisfying $Q^T Q = I$.
Expressing a symmetric matrix as a sum of rank-one projection matrices weighted by its eigenvalues.
The number of times an eigenvalue appears as a root of the characteristic polynomial.

example.title: Spectral Decomposition of a 2x2 Matrix
example.body: Consider the symmetric matrix $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$. Step 1: Find eigenvalues by solving $\det(A - \lambda I) = (2-\lambda)^2 - 1 = 0$. This gives $\lambda_1 = 3$ and $\lambda_2 = 1$. Step 2: For $\lambda_1 = 3$, solve $\begin{bmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix} x = 0$, giving eigenvector $v_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$. Normalized, $x_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1/\sqrt{2} \\ 1/\sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix}$. Step 3: For $\lambda_2 = 1$, solve $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} x = 0$, giving eigenvector $v_2 = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$. Normalized, $x_2 = \begin{bmatrix} -1/\sqrt{2} \\ 1/\sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix}$. Step 4: The spectral decomposition is $A = 3 x_1 x_1^T + 1 x_2 x_2^T$, which expands to $3 \begin{bmatrix} 1/2 & 1/2 \\ 1/2 & 1/2 \end{bmatrix} + 1 \begin{bmatrix} 1/2 & -1/2 \\ -1/2 & 1/2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$.

exam_tips: Always check if the given matrix is symmetric before applying the spectral theorem shortcuts.
Remember to normalize all eigenvectors to unit length; unnormalized $Q$ is not orthogonal.
For repeated eigenvalues, explicitly show the Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization steps to earn full marks.
Verify your final decomposition by multiplying back $Q \Lambda Q^T$ to match the original matrix.
mistakes: Assuming eigenvectors of distinct eigenvalues are already orthogonal without checking numerical scaling.
Forgetting to divide eigenvectors by their magnitudes to form the orthonormal matrix $Q$.
Writing $A = Q \Lambda Q$ instead of the correct orthogonal relation $A = Q \Lambda Q^T$.

en.title: Positive Definite Matrices
en.summary: A positive definite matrix is a symmetric matrix with strictly positive eigenvalues, serving as the matrix equivalent of a positive real number. They are crucial in optimization, guaranteeing a strict local minimum, and appear frequently in both semester exams and GATE.

sections.heading: Core Definition and Physical Analogy
sections.body: Think of a positive definite matrix $A$ as the multidimensional curvature of a bowl-shaped surface given by the quadratic form $f(x) = x^T A x$. Just like a parabola $y = ax^2$ opens upward when $a > 0$, a symmetric matrix $A$ represents an upward-curving paraboloid if and only if it is positive definite. Formally, an $n \times n$ symmetric matrix $A$ is positive definite if $x^T A x > 0$ for all non-zero vectors $x$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$. In your B.Tech exams, you will be asked to test whether a given matrix is positive definite using multiple equivalent conditions.

sections.heading: The Four Tests for Positive Definiteness
sections.body: To determine if a matrix $A$ is positive definite, you can use any of the following four equivalent conditions: First, all eigenvalues of $A$ must be strictly positive, i.e., $\lambda_i > 0$ for all $i$. Second, all pivots obtained during elimination without row exchanges must be positive, i.e., $d_i > 0$. Third, all leading principal minors (determinants of the top-left $k \times k$ submatrices) must be strictly positive. Fourth, the matrix can be factored as $A = L D L^T$ where all entries on the diagonal of $D$ are positive. In exams, Sylvester's criterion (using leading principal minors) and the eigenvalue test are the most frequently used.

sections.heading: Sylvester's Criterion Algorithm
sections.body: To apply Sylvester's Criterion on an $n \times n$ matrix $A$, follow these exact steps: Step 1: Extract the $1 \times 1$ top-left submatrix $M_1 = [a_{11}]$ and compute its determinant. It must be greater than zero. Step 2: Extract the $2 \times 2$ top-left submatrix $M_2 = \begin{bmatrix} a_{11} & a_{12} \\ a_{21} & a_{22} \end{bmatrix}$ and compute its determinant. It must be strictly positive. Step 3: Continue this process up to $M_n = A$, ensuring every leading principal minor $\det(M_k) > 0$ for $k = 1, 2, \dots, n$. If even one minor is less than or equal to zero, the matrix is not positive definite.

key_terms.meaning: A symmetric matrix whose quadratic form is strictly positive for all non-zero vectors.
A scalar function of vectors defined by $x^T A x$.
The determinant of the top-left $k \times k$ submatrix of a square matrix.
A theorem stating a matrix is positive definite iff all its leading principal minors are positive.
The leading entry in a row during Gaussian elimination before scaling.

example.title: Testing a 2x2 Matrix for Positive Definiteness
example.body: Consider the matrix $A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -2 \\ -2 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$. We will test it using leading principal minors. Step 1: Find the first leading principal minor $M_1 = 4$. Since $4 > 0$, the first condition is satisfied. Step 2: Find the second leading principal minor $M_2 = \det \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -2 \\ -2 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$. Calculating this gives $(4)(5) - (-2)(-2) = 20 - 4 = 16$. Since $16 > 0$, the second condition is satisfied. Since all leading principal minors are strictly positive, $A$ is positive definite. Alternatively, checking eigenvalues: $\det(A - \lambda I) = (\lambda - 4)(\lambda - 5) - 4 = \lambda^2 - 9\lambda + 16 = 0$. Solving yields positive eigenvalues, confirming the result.

exam_tips: Always check if the matrix is symmetric first; non-symmetric matrices cannot be classified as positive definite in standard curriculum.
When using Sylvester's criterion, write down the submatrices explicitly to secure step marks.
For GATE, remember that the sum of positive definite matrices is also positive definite, but the product is not necessarily symmetric or positive definite.
mistakes: Confusing positive definite ($\lambda > 0$) with positive semi-definite ($\lambda \ge 0$).
Computing arbitrary minors instead of leading principal minors (top-left aligned ones).
Forgetting to verify symmetry before applying eigenvalue or minor tests.

en.title: Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)
en.summary: Singular Value Decomposition factorizes any real $m \times n$ matrix $A$ into $U \Sigma V^T$, revealing fundamental geometric and structural properties. It is crucial for dimensionality reduction, pseudoinverses, and appears frequently in both university semester exams and GATE.

sections.heading: Concept and Geometric Meaning
sections.body: Think of SVD as breaking down a complex transformation into three simpler actions: a rotation $V^T$, a stretching along orthogonal axes $\Sigma$, and another rotation $U$. For any $m \times n$ matrix $A$, SVD writes $A = U \Sigma V^T$. Here, $U$ is an $m \times m$ orthogonal matrix whose columns are the left-singular vectors (eigenvectors of $A A^T$). $V$ is an $n \times n$ orthogonal matrix whose columns are the right-singular vectors (eigenvectors of $A^T A$). $\Sigma$ is an $m \times n$ diagonal matrix containing the singular values $\sigma_i$, arranged in descending order $\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \dots \ge 0$. The non-zero singular values are the square roots of the non-zero eigenvalues of $A^T A$.

sections.heading: Step-by-Step Algorithm
sections.body: To compute the SVD of an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ manually for exams, follow these exact steps. First, compute the symmetric matrix $A^T A$ of size $n \times n$. Second, find the eigenvalues of $A^T A$ by solving $\det(A^T A - \lambda I) = 0$. Order them as $\lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_n \ge 0$. The singular values are $\sigma_i = \sqrt{\lambda_i}$. Third, find the orthonormal eigenvectors $v_1, v_2, \dots, v_n$ of $A^T A$. These form the columns of the orthogonal matrix $V$. Fourth, construct the first $r$ columns of $U$ (where $r$ is the rank of $A$) using the formula $u_i = \frac{1}{\sigma_i} A v_i$. Fifth, extend this set to form a complete orthonormal basis for $\mathbb{R}^m$ using the Gram-Schmidt process if $m > r$, completing the matrix $U$.

sections.heading: Conventions and Tie-Breaking in Exams
sections.body: When solving numerical problems, strict conventions must be followed to secure full marks. Singular values $\sigma_i$ must always be listed in non-increasing order: $\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \dots \ge \sigma_r > 0$. If $A^T A$ yields repeated eigenvalues, ensure you use the Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization process on the resulting eigenspaces to construct an orthonormal set of eigenvectors for $V$. When computing $u_i = \frac{1}{\sigma_i} A v_i$, maintain exact radical forms rather than decimals unless specified. If $m < n$, it is often computationally faster to start with $A A^T$ to find $U$ and $\Sigma$ first, then derive $V$, but always state your method clearly in the exam script.

key_terms.meaning: Square root of an eigenvalue of $A^T A$, denoted by $\sigma_i$.
Eigenvector of $A A^T$, forming the columns of orthogonal matrix $U$.
Eigenvector of $A^T A$, forming the columns of orthogonal matrix $V$.
Generalized inverse of a matrix computed via SVD as $V \Sigma^+ U^T$.

example.title: Manual SVD of a 2x1 Matrix
example.body: Let $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$. We want to find $A = U \Sigma V^T$. First, compute $A^T A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \end{bmatrix}$. The eigenvalue of $A^T A$ is $\lambda_1 = 2$. Thus, the singular value is $\sigma_1 = \sqrt{2}$. The matrix $\Sigma$ is $2 \times 1$, given by $\Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} \sqrt{2} \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$. For $V$, the $1 \times 1$ matrix is $V = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \end{bmatrix}$ since $v_1^2 = 1$. Next, compute $u_1 = \frac{1}{\sigma_1} A v_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1/\sqrt{2} \\ 1/\sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix}$. To complete $U$ ($2 \times 2$), we find an orthogonal vector to $u_1$, which is $u_2 = \begin{bmatrix} -1/\sqrt{2} \\ 1/\sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix}$. Thus, $U = \begin{bmatrix} 1/\sqrt{2} & -1/\sqrt{2} \\ 1/\sqrt{2} & 1/\sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix}$. The SVD is $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1/\sqrt{2} & -1/\sqrt{2} \\ 1/\sqrt{2} & 1/\sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \sqrt{2} \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \end{bmatrix}$.

exam_tips: Always verify your intermediate matrices by checking if $U$ and $V$ are truly orthogonal ($U^T U = I$).
Arrange singular values in strictly descending order; placing them out of order results in an immediate deduction.
For GATE, remember that the rank of $A$ equals the number of non-zero singular values.
Show the characteristic equation $\det(A^T A - \lambda I) = 0$ clearly step-by-step.
mistakes: Forgetting to normalize the eigenvectors when constructing $U$ and $V$.
Confusing $A^T A$ with $A A^T$ when starting the algorithm for non-square matrices.
Failing to apply Gram-Schmidt when repeated eigenvalues occur in symmetric matrices.
